name: BloodHound GUI - Start Neo4j and BloodHound
description: Starts the Neo4j graph database backend and launches the BloodHound GUI. Neo4j must be running before BloodHound can connect. Default creds: neo4j/neo4j (must change on first login). After login, drag-and-drop the JSON/ZIP files from BloodHound.py or SharpHound to import data and run attack-path queries.
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== STARTUP SEQUENCE ===
1. sudo neo4j start
   - Wait for 'Started.' message before launching BloodHound
   - Neo4j web UI: http://localhost:7474 (optional, for debugging)
   - Default bolt: bolt://localhost:7687

2. bloodhound (or click the app)
   - Connect to: bolt://localhost:7687
   - Username: neo4j
   - Password: neo4j → forced to change on first login

3. Import data: drag-and-drop all JSON files or the .zip from BloodHound.py/SharpHound

=== KEY QUERIES TO RUN FIRST ===
In the BloodHound search bar, click 'Queries' (pre-built):
  'Find all Domain Admins'               → who is DA?
  'Shortest Paths to Domain Admins'      → attack paths from owned users
  'Find Principals with DCSync Rights'   → who can DCSync?
  'Kerberoastable Accounts'              → ranked by encryption type
  'AS-REP Roastable Accounts'            → no preauth required
  'Find Workstations where DA logged on' → DA session hunting

=== MARKING OWNED NODES ===
Right-click any node → 'Mark User as Owned' (skull icon appears)
Then run: 'Shortest Paths from Owned Principals to Domain Admins'
This shows your personalized attack path from your current creds.

=== BLOODHOUND COMMUNITY EDITION (CE) ===
Newer BloodHound CE uses Docker instead of Neo4j directly:
  sudo docker-compose up
Connects to http://localhost:8080 (not a separate app)
Pre-built queries are in the 'Cypher' tab
Lab exercises typically use classic BloodHound unless specified.

=== CYPHER QUERIES (custom) ===
Example — find users who can write to any group:
  MATCH p=(u:User)-[:GenericWrite|WriteOwner|WriteDacl]->(g:Group) RETURN p
Example — all paths to Enterprise Admins:
  MATCH p=shortestPath((n)-[*1..]->(m:Group {name:'ENTERPRISE ADMINS@INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL'})) RETURN p Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 21 (Active Directory Introduction and Enumeration).

recommended.note: SharpHound must be run first to collect AD data.

defense.why_it_works: Starting neo4j and the BloodHound GUI ingests collected data and computes attack paths (shortest path to Domain Admins, ACL abuse chains).
defense.prerequisites: Collected SharpHound/bloodhound-python data on the attacker host.
defense.impact: Visualised, queryable attack paths across the domain - offline analysis on the attacker box.
defense.detection: Runs on the attacker host analysing already-collected data - no target interaction at this step.
defense.artifacts: A local neo4j database of the collected graph; no victim-side artifact.
defense.prevention: Prevention is upstream (detect the collection); this analysis is offline and undetectable by the victim.
defense.misconfiguration: Active Directory's default read ACL allows any authenticated domain user to enumerate nearly the entire directory: all user accounts, groups, SPNs, computer objects, trust relationships, and many sensitive attributes. There is no built-in 'need to know' principle on LDAP reads. BloodHound, PowerView, and ldapsearch all exploit these open default ACLs to map attack paths.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# AD default permissions — authenticated users can read:
# All user objects: sAMAccountName, userPrincipalName, memberOf, servicePrincipalName
# All computer objects: DNS names, OS versions, operating system attributes
# All group memberships, GPOs, OU structure, domain trusts

# Verify with any low-priv account:
Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties *  # returns all users + attributes
Get-ADGroup -Filter * | Get-ADGroupMember  # all group memberships
defense.secure_config:
# 1. Enable AD Recycle Bin + Protected Users group
# 2. Audit and tighten ACLs on sensitive attributes:
#    msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo, adminCount, memberOf for privileged groups

# 3. Disable SMB null sessions + restrict LDAP anonymous binds (see smb/ldap cards)

# 4. Detect enumeration via volume:
# Sysmon Event 3 (network connection) from non-DC to DC on port 389/636
# Event 4661 — access to SAM objects (high-volume; baseline first)
# Microsoft Defender for Identity: 'Account Enumeration Reconnaissance' alert

# 5. Deploy Honey accounts/objects:
# Fake high-priv account (no real access) — any LDAP query for it = attacker
# BloodHound run from non-DC = detectable via DC LDAP traffic volume

# 6. Tiered administration: Tier 0 DCs, Tier 1 servers, Tier 2 workstations
#    Each tier can only query its own tier's objects

variations.label: Reset neo4j password on first run
